title: SpaceX Wants a Million AI Satellites in Orbit. Scientists Say It Could Damage Earth's Climate
excerpt: The plan for solar-powered orbital data centers promises unlimited AI compute but raises serious questions about atmospheric pollution, ozone depletion and space debris.
body:
• SpaceX has filed with the FCC to launch up to one million satellites for orbital AI data centers, dwarfing the roughly 14,500 active satellites currently in orbit.
  • Scientists warn that rocket launches and satellite re-entries at this scale would accelerate ozone depletion and upper-atmosphere warming from soot and alumina particles.
  • SpaceX aims for 1 gigawatt of orbital compute by end of 2027, scaling to 1 terawatt by 2030 — requiring millions of satellites based on its AI1 satellite design.
  • NASA Administrator has expressed openness to space-based data centers, while critics call the plan "greenwashing" that shifts environmental costs rather than eliminating them.

SpaceX's proposal to place up to one million AI data center satellites in orbit has set off a sharp debate among scientists, regulators and space industry watchers over what the plan would mean for Earth's climate and the sustainability of low-Earth orbit.

The company filed an application with the Federal Communications Commission in January 2026 seeking permission for the massive constellation, which would use solar power to run AI workloads and link back to Earth through SpaceX's existing Starlink network. In its FCC filing, SpaceX argued the satellites would "achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers."

Scientists say the reality is far more complicated.

The Climate Problem

Each rocket launch produces substantial emissions, and scaling to the cadence SpaceX envisions would multiply the impact dramatically. A single Starship launch burns roughly a kiloton of liquid methane, producing climate pollution comparable to a small city's annual output.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=4kGT_b77MYA

The bigger concern is where those emissions go. Black carbon soot deposited in the upper atmosphere can persist for up to four years, far longer than the same particles at ground level. Water vapor from rocket exhaust also acts as a potent greenhouse gas at altitude.

"Soot that comes out of the tailpipe in a car normally lasts maybe a few weeks in the lower atmosphere. But when you put it into the upper atmosphere, it could stay there for years."

— Peter Howson, Northumbria University

Then there is the end-of-life problem. SpaceX satellites have an approximately five-year shelf life before they are deorbited and incinerated in the atmosphere. The resulting alumina particles — metal dust from burning spacecraft — have already been detected in the stratosphere. Scientists warn these particles contribute to ozone depletion, and at the scale of a million satellites cycling through re-entry, the cumulative effect is poorly understood.

The Scale Challenge

SpaceX's S-1 filing ahead of its June 2026 IPO outlined an ambitious roadmap: 1 gigawatt of orbital compute capacity by end of 2027, scaling to 10 GW by 2028, 100 GW by 2029 and 1 terawatt by 2030. Based on the company's AI1 satellite design, which produces roughly 150 kilowatts per unit, reaching 1 terawatt would require approximately 6.7 million satellites.

To build them, SpaceX is constructing an 11-million-square-foot factory called "Gigasat" in Bastrop, Texas, handling everything from solar panel production to satellite assembly. The company listed the orbital compute initiative among its principal risk factors in the IPO filing, cautioning it "may not achieve commercial viability."

The Case For and Against

NASA Administrator Bill Nelson has expressed openness to the concept, suggesting space-based data centers could make sense given the energy constraints facing terrestrial AI infrastructure. Startup Starcloud launched the first satellite carrying an Nvidia H100 GPU in November 2025 and trained an LLM in orbit the following month.

But critics see fundamental problems. Solar panels degrade faster in space due to radiation. Microchips are vulnerable to "bit flipping" from high-energy particles. Cooling in the vacuum of space is harder, not easier, than on Earth — there is no air to carry heat away, forcing reliance on radiators that add weight and complexity.

A Brookings Institution analysis called the plan a potential exercise in "greenwashing," warning it could generate more space debris, increase collision risk and ruin the night sky — all while shifting environmental costs rather than eliminating them.

The Kessler Problem

Perhaps the most sobering concern is the Kessler syndrome: a cascading chain of orbital collisions where debris from one collision creates more debris, triggering further collisions. With a million satellites in low-Earth orbit, even tiny failure rates could produce large-scale debris events that hinder space activities for decades.

The FCC is still reviewing SpaceX's application. With only about 14,500 active satellites currently in orbit worldwide, the proposal would represent a roughly 70-fold increase — and the environmental review framework for such a scale simply does not exist yet.
